claims.text: The starting catalyst is a near-equiatomic multi-principal-element automotive alloy with minimal platinum-group-metal content.
The proposed intervention is addition of 1–3 atomic percent Pd to the catalyst.
Adding Pd will lower the light-off temperature for CO oxidation relative to the unmodified catalyst.
Adding Pd will lower the light-off temperature for hydrocarbon oxidation relative to the unmodified catalyst.
Adding Pd will reduce inhibition or poisoning by H2O.
Adding Pd will reduce inhibition or poisoning by NO.
Adding Pd will improve retention of oxidation activity after accelerated aging.
Low-level Pd addition will form Pd–Cu interfaces in the alloy microstructure.
Pd–Cu interfaces will modify the catalyst's electronic properties.
Pd–Cu interfaces will stabilize oxidation-active sites.
Introduced Pd will facilitate redox cycling.
Introduced Pd will promote preferential adsorption and oxidation of H2O and NO as poisoning species.
Pd will synergize with Cu sites to lower oxidation activation barriers.
The proposed effects will persist during transient operation below 150 °C in exhaust containing H2O and NO.
The proposed effects will persist after aging intended to simulate vehicle-lifetime mileage.
Pd contents below approximately 5 atomic percent are expected to retain the beneficial effects.
Higher Pd contents might compromise low platinum-group-metal usage and alter the alloy characteristics.
The Pd addition can maintain low-temperature activity without increasing overall platinum-group-metal use.

contradictions.description: The intervention explicitly adds 1–3 atomic percent Pd, a platinum-group metal, while the mechanism claims this occurs without increasing overall platinum-group-metal use. No compensating removal or replacement of another platinum-group metal is specified.
